briefs.polymarket-5699271: The question asks whether the October 2026 seasonally adjusted core CPI-U one-month change, as printed to one decimal by BLS on 2026-11-10 (https://www.bls.gov/schedule/news_release/cpi.htm), will be exactly 0.2 percent. The base rate comes from the BLS series (https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/CUSR0000SA0L1E?output_view=pct_1mth): from January 2016 through September 2026, skipping the two unavailable 2025 months, 46 of 127 monthly prints were 0.2, about 36 percent, and only 2 of 9 published Octobers (2018 and 2019) were 0.2. The 2026 prints for March to September were 0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0.0, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.3 (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm, 2026-10-14), so 0.2 has come up in three of seven months. The Cleveland Fed nowcast of 0.21 (https://www.clevelandfed.org/indicators-and-data/inflation-nowcasting, 2026-11-05) points to 0.2, but its own FAQ describes it as a 12-month moving average of past core inflation that does not observe October prices, so it was given little weight. The September report showed broad firmness: owners' equivalent rent up 0.3, shelter 0.4, used cars 0.7, airfares 1.2, services 0.4, and core excluding shelter up 0.3 in July, August and September (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.t03.htm). The September producer price index for final demand less foods, energy and trade services rose 0.5 percent (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/ppi_10152026.htm, 2026-10-15), and the FOMC held rates on 2026-10-28 with two dissents in favor of a hike (https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm). Together this makes 0.3 the most likely print, with 0.2 second, while the long-run frequency of about 36 percent is tempered by the firm recent run. No consensus survey was available in the research. A softer shelter reading, a drop in used car or airfare prices, or a consensus near 0.2 published before the release would favor 0.2, while another broad 0.3 pace would point away from it.
briefs.manifold-gq5RCCO6PN: The question asks whether T Coronae Borealis reaches visual magnitude 5.0 or brighter before 2026-11-11 00:00 ET, as reported by sources such as AAVSO. The reference class is thin: Schaefer's compiled light curve for 1842 to 2022 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04933) shows only two primary eruptions, 1866 and 1946, both peaking at V=2.0, about 80 years apart, and each stayed within 3 magnitudes of peak for roughly 5 to 6 days, so the star spent perhaps 10 to 12 days at magnitude 5 or brighter in 156 years. The 1866 eruption rose faster than one magnitude per hour, and AAVSO notes a 1946-like eruption could take the star from about V=9.8 to about V=1.7 in under a day (https://aavso.org/blog/what-to-do-during-the-eruption-of-t-crb/, 2025-11-20), so any eruption starting in the window would qualify. The star is now overdue by the 80-year rule: an arXiv analysis through 2026-07-11 (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.15245) puts the interval at 80.415 years with no eruption, and EarthSky on 2026-11-03 (https://earthsky.org/space/blaze-star-nova-corona-borealis-how-to-see-it/) says earlier predicted dates in 2025 passed without one. On 2026-11-05 an AAVSO observer measured it at B=11.235 (https://theskylive.com/sky/stars/hr-5958-star), still quiescent, and a separate visual series stayed near V=9.9 to 10.4 through 2026-10-28. The paper's nearer timing guess points to around December 2026, after the cutoff. Even treating the eruption as a 30 to 50 percent a year event given how overdue it is, the share of that falling in a five-day window is under one percent, so the window is very short against the evidence. An AAVSO alert, a reported brightening above magnitude 9, or a confirmed multi-source detection before 2026-11-11 would change the answer.
briefs.manifold-RZUdPgyPN5: The question asks whether the market creator will find it true that neural networks are already clean, a judgment based on the Goodfire essay by Nick Cammarata and others and on the surrounding discussion, with the market closing 2026-11-15 (the resolver says he is not an expert). The base reference class is the three main interpretability papers that addressed the question, Zoom In (2020-03-10, https://distill.pub/2020/circuits/zoom-in/), Toy Models of Superposition (2022-09-21, https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652) and the sparse-autoencoder paper arXiv:2309.08600, none of which concluded that neurons are clean, so the prior is 0 of 3 and the question was worked out as a strong claim needing unusual support. The essay (https://already-clean.goodfire.com/, revised 2026-10-30) is a working hypothesis: a held-out check on 183 Qwen3-32B neurons found explanation-based examples fired strongly 76 percent of the time against 11 percent for near misses and about 1 percent for distant concepts, a GPT-2 XL re-audit found about 70 percent of neurons looking like one thing against under 2 percent called clean in 2023, and the authors say they are maybe 85 percent sure of a change in kind and that the title overstates the evidence. MIT Technology Review covered it on 2026-10-19 and Transluce showed neuron-basis circuits as sparse as SAE circuits in Llama 3.1-8B (2025-11-20, https://transluce.org/neuron-circuits). Against it, Liv Gorton reported on 2026-10-20 that her replications disagreed and the canonical cat-and-car cases did not survive basic checks (https://livgorton.com/already-clean-thoughts/), and Andriy Batutin reported on 2026-10-19 that 84 percent of untrained random-init Qwen3 neurons were labelled single-job against 52 percent of trained ones, with none of 299 trained neurons meeting his pre-registered bar (https://andriybatutin.substack.com/p/we-tried-to-confirm-neural-networks). The technical companion paper had not appeared by 2026-11-06. The mixed record of strong claims by the authors and failed independent checks argues for caution about the strong form of the claim. A released companion paper with independent replication, or a clear endorsement by other interpretability groups before 2026-11-15, would strengthen the case; further failed controls would weaken it.
